title: A rule for life
hookLine: after five years, a lasting rule: small, steady, yours
tomorrow: morning or night: when does prayer actually stick?

cards: Resolutions have a short shelf life: the gym pass, the journal with three entries, the app streak that broke on a Tuesday. Usually it isn't willpower that's missing. It's a shape.

Here's an odd detail from someone who built something that lasted. Saint Benedict wrote a rule that Benedictine monasteries still live by. Near the end of it, he calls it a little rule written for beginners.
Why would its author call it that?

teach.h: NOT A FINISH LINE: A TRELLIS.
teach.b: Because a rule of life isn't a finish line. It's a trellis, something to grow on.
In his prologue, Benedict says he hopes to set down nothing harsh and nothing burdensome. A rule is what you do on ordinary days, so the hard days have something to stand on.
Most of Benedict's rule is ordinary: when to pray, when to eat, when to sleep, how to treat a guest. One chapter says every guest should be welcomed as Christ. And the Church's first rule was tiny.
Acts says the first believers "were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers."
Teaching, bread, prayer, together. A rule in one sentence. So how do you write yours after five years?
Not by copying a saint's schedule.
Start with what already works: the prayer you actually say, the Mass you actually go to, the friend you actually call.
Benedict built on what people could keep. Over the next days this block takes the pieces one at a time: daily prayer, Sunday, confession, scripture, service. Today is only the inventory.

how: Many religious orders live by a written rule, and lay Catholics often keep a simple personal rule of life, sometimes with a spiritual director, naming their daily prayer, Sunday Mass, confession and service.

games.q: what does “a rule for life” mean?
o: a steady pattern of prayer and practice you keep
a list of church laws every Catholic must obey
a strict set of vows that only monks can take

games.q: what's inside a rule — tap the pairs.
p: the first believers' rule in Acts

s: a rule of life is only for monks and nuns
Acts gives the first believers' rule in one sentence: teaching, bread, prayer.
Benedict called his rule a little rule for beginners
near its end. a rule isn't a finish line.
a good rule starts with the hardest practices you can manage
Benedict hoped for nothing harsh; start with what already works.

games.q: your aunt starts a rule of life: up at five for an hour of prayer, daily Mass, a fast twice a week. it's day two. what would Benedict suggest?
o: start from what she already keeps, and add slowly.
go all in, since a rule only counts if it's hard.
wait until she's holier before trying any rule.
games.why: Benedict wrote a little rule for beginners, with nothing harsh or burdensome. a rule grows from what already works.

practice: Find a scrap of paper and write down three things that already hold you up: a prayer, a habit, a person, a place. Don't add anything new yet. Look at the list until the bell, and notice how much is already there.
Leave it where you'll see it.

wordCard.voice: A rule for life. A small, steady pattern of prayer and practice, built on what already works.

orig.note: Latin: a rule. Benedict's book is the Regula, his rule for monks.

carryVoice: The line to keep: what works, the place to build from instead of scratch. See you tomorrow.
